The package has one main object. You build a `LongRunRisksModel`, you
solve it, and you read the results. Everything else on this page is
either a way to build the model from data or a way to get the raw data
in the first place.

```python
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
import tidyfinance as tf
import lrrcs as lrr

model = lrr.LongRunRisksModel()      # the Table II calibration
res = model.solve()                  # solve on the state grid
print(res.summary())                 # returns, betas, log P/D
res.value_premium                    # 5.18
```

<!-- API page cross-checked against `lrr.__all__` (20 names)
     via `python -c "import lrrcs as lrr; print(*lrr.__all__)"`. Sections below
     cover all of them. New public names must be added here in the same PR. -->

`market` is the time-series claim. `long` and `short` are the two legs
of a sort. `value` and `growth` remain aliases, so the paper's names
keep working without any extra arguments.

## The model

| Member | Signature | What it does |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `LongRunRisksModel` | `(params=None, *, delta=None, gamma=None, psi=None, mu=None, rho=None, phi_x=None, sigma=None, nu=None, sigma_w=None, claims=None, long=None, short=None, market=None, residual_corr=None)` | The model specification. Defaults to Table II. |
| `.solve` | `(method="grid", *, n_x=30, n_s=4, max_iter=200_000, tol=1e-10, pd_anchor=None, pd_anchor_c=None)` | `GridResults` or `AnalyticalResults` |
| `.simulate` | `(n_samples=1000, years=74, *, seed=0, burn_in_years=5, n_x=30, n_s=4)` | `SimulationResults`: the paper's Table VII |
| `.simulate_cashflows` | `(n_sims=200, years=74, seed=42)` | cash-flow moments only, no prices (Tables III to V) |
| `.simulate_paths` | `(months, *, seed=None)` | one simulated path of $x_t$, $\sigma_t^2$, and growth rates |
| `.replace` | `(**kwargs)` | a new model with some arguments changed |
| `.from_loading` | `(phi, *, mu=0.0015, phi_sigma=7.5, alpha=0.5, name="claim", params=None)` | one synthetic claim from its cash-flow loading ([Chapter 11](../chapters/11-price-your-own-claim.qmd)) |
| `.from_cashflows` | `(dc, claims=None, *, long=None, short=None, market=None, frequency="annual", window=2, default_phi_sigma=7.5, params=None)` | calibrate the claims from growth series ([Chapter 8](../chapters/08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd)) |

The two methods answer different questions. `method="grid"` solves the
Euler equations on the Tauchen-Hussey state space and is where the
paper's numbers come from. `method="analytical"` is the log-linear
approximation of Section 3.4. It is instant, and it is the right tool
for reading loadings and prices of risk.

Solving never changes the model, so a counterfactual is a new model
rather than an edited one:

```python
lrr.LongRunRisksModel(gamma=7.5).solve().value_premium
model.replace(claims={"value": {"phi": 2.6}}).solve().value_premium
```

A claim given only some of its four fields keeps the rest of the
calibration. Naming a claim the default does not have replaces the
whole cross-section instead, and then all four fields are required.

## Results

Every solve and simulation returns an object of this shape. Quantities
that vary by claim are `pandas.Series` indexed by claim name.
Quantities that describe the whole model are floats. Returns, premia,
and rates are annualized and in percent.

| Attribute | On | Meaning |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `expected_returns`, `volatility`, `sharpe_ratios`, `capm_betas` | grid, simulation | annual return moments by claim |
| `mean_log_pd`, `price_dividend` / `pd_levels` | all three | valuation ratios by claim |
| `risk_free`, `value_premium` | all three | the rate and the long-short spread |
| `log_pd_spread` | grid | long leg minus short leg log P/D |
| `converged`, `n_x`, `n_s` | grid | how the solve went |
| `z_c`, `z`, `stationary`, `x_nodes`, `s2_nodes`, `states()` | grid | the solved valuation functions and the grid under them |
| `A1`, `A2`, `long_run_premium`, `expected_growth`, `gordon_return` | analytical | loadings and the long-run piece of compensation |
| `risk_prices`, `Lambda_eta`, `Lambda_eps`, `Lambda_w` | analytical | prices of the three shocks |
| `expected_returns_se`, `volatility_se`, `mean_log_pd_se`, `beta_ratio` | simulation | cross-sample dispersion and the beta ratio |
| `summary()` | all three | a formatted table you can print |
| `to_frame()` | all three | a tidy frame, one row per claim |

`long_short_premium` is an alias of `value_premium` for cross-sections
that are not value and growth. `to_frame()` and `states()` follow the
`tidyfinance` backend, so they return polars frames when you set it.

## Measure loadings from cash flows

These stay separate because they are the step that must not see
returns. Nothing here has an argument that could accept one.

| Function | Signature | Returns |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `expected_growth_proxy` | `(dc, window=2) -> ndarray` | moving average of lagged consumption growth (the $x_t$ proxy) |
| `filter_expected_growth` | `(dc) -> dict` | Kalman/MLE $\hat x_t$; `mu, rho, q, r, loglik, x` |
| `estimate_long_run_leverage` | `(dc, dd, window=2) -> float` | $\tilde\phi$: slope of dividend growth on the MA |
| `lrr.calibration.calibrate_from_data` | `(dc, dd_dict=None, frequency="annual", window=2, default_phi_sigma=7.5, *, long=None, short=None, market=None) -> dict[str, DividendParams]` | monthly dividend parameters from annual data |

`LongRunRisksModel.from_cashflows` wraps the last one and hands back a
model you can solve directly.

## Data construction

| Function | Signature | Returns |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `load_consumption` | `() -> pd.Series` | real per-capita ND+S growth, 1930 to 2003 |
| `load_deflator` | `() -> pd.Series` | PCE deflator |
| `real_rf_from_monthly` | `(t90, cpi) -> pd.Series` | annual real T-bill from monthly |
| `campbell_shiller_annual` | `(ret, retx, defl) -> pd.DataFrame` | real dividends and price index from CRSP returns |
| `build_annual_panel` | `(refresh=False, start=1930, end=2003) -> pl.DataFrame` | growth/value/market panel |
| `table_i` | `(bm, start=1930, end=2003) -> pd.DataFrame` | Table I statistics |
| `table_vi_data` | `(bm, dc, start=1930, end=2003) -> pd.DataFrame` | Table VI loadings |
| `EmpiricalDataError` | exception | raised when WRDS credentials are missing |

`lrr.empirical.consumption_growth_from_levels(nd, sv, pop)` builds the
consumption series from its NIPA components.

## Figures

The paper's figures live in the subpackages, since the chapters build
their own plots with plotnine.

| Function | Signature |
|:---|:---|
| `lrr.empirical.figure1` … `figure4` | `(data, path)` |
| `lrrcs.implications.figures.figure5` | `(path, years=1000, seed=1)` |
| `lrrcs.implications.figures.figure_lr_premium` | `(path)` |
| `lrrcs.implications.figures.figure_mean_pd` | `(results, path)` |

## Parameters and errors

`ModelParams`, `PreferencesParams`, `ConsumptionParams`, and
`DividendParams` are the parameter dataclasses. `ModelParams()` is the
Table II calibration, so you rarely need to build one by hand.
`SolverDivergenceError` is raised when a fixed point leaves the
plausible range, which usually means the grid is too coarse for the
calibration. `EmpiricalDataError` is raised when WRDS credentials are
missing, with a message telling you to call `tf.set_wrds_credentials()`.

The subpackages `lrrcs.model`, `lrrcs.implications`,
`lrrcs.calibration`, and `lrrcs.empirical` hold the machinery under all
of this. They are importable, and the two calibration and data entries
above are the only places the documented path reaches into them.

## A new sort, end to end

Consumption and two dividend legs go in. No returns enter.

```python
dc = pl.read_csv("data/consumption_annual.csv").sort("year")["dc"].to_numpy()
panel = pl.read_csv("data/annual_panel.csv")

def dd(claim):
    return (
        panel.filter(pl.col("claim") == claim)
        .sort("year")["dgrowth"]
        .to_numpy()
    )

model = lrr.LongRunRisksModel.from_cashflows(
    dc,
    long=dd("Value"),
    short=dd("Growth"),
    market=dd("Market"),
    frequency="annual",
    window=2,
)
print(model.solve().summary())
```

The premium that comes out was never targeted, which is what makes the
comparison with the data a test rather than a fit.
